source_metadata.title: Topical gel-based biomaterials for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers
source_metadata.source_type: narrative review of topical gel-based biomaterials for diabetic foot ulcers

extraction_metadata.scope_note: This source is a narrative review, not primary literature. Cited study findings are retained as secondary reports and tagged secondary_reported_result. Bibliographic entries were not atomized. Primary-study claims require direct extraction from the cited publications before downstream use as primary evidence.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aims to identify topical biomaterial gel approaches for chronic diabetic foot ulcer healing in animal models and clinical trials, with emphasis on protein or peptide, drug, cellular, herbal or antioxidant, and nanoparticle or microparticle strategies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The goal of this review is to identify different treatment approaches using topical biomaterial gels for diabetic wound healing in both animal models and clinical trials.

atoms.canonical_statement: For this review, topical biomaterial gels were defined as injectable viscous materials that can be applied by syringes, pipettes, tubes, or similar methods; biomaterial dressings and highly cross-linked preformed hydrogels requiring surgical implantation were excluded.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Topical biomaterial gels for the purpose of this review are defined as any injectable viscous gel material that can be applied using syringes, pipettes, tubes etc. and are easily applied on the wound.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review contrasts acute wound healing with chronic diabetic wound healing, describing chronic wounds as having delayed immune-cell recruitment, impaired neutrophil clearance, prolonged inflammatory activity, excessive matrix metalloproteinase activity, poor angiogenesis, hypoxia, and impaired collagen and epidermal development.

Natural biomaterials can mimic native tissue and support cell attachment and infiltration with relatively favorable biocompatibility, but the review notes rapid enzymatic degradation and weak mechanical properties as limits.

Synthetic biomaterials permit broad chemical modification of crosslinking density, mechanical strength, degradation, and drug delivery, but the review notes lower bioactivity, weaker tissue integration, low biodegradability, and greater inflammatory potential.
The review identifies ease of application, less invasive delivery, direct therapeutic contact with the wound, and avoidance of systemic delivery as advantages of topical gels.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Benefits of topical gels over other treatment approaches include ease of application, less invasive delivery method, increased direct contact of therapeutic with the wound, and avoidance of systemic delivery of therapeutics.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review identifies limited mechanical strength and increased degradation rate as core limitations of topical gels.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: limitations to the use of topical gels, including limited mechanical strength and increased degradation rate

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that many preclinical topical gel approaches have not reached the clinic and identifies gel design, market need, manufacturing cost, and regulatory requirements as translation barriers.
The review notes that complicated chemical modifications, added purification steps, expensive raw materials, and restricted raw-material supply can make gel manufacturing and scale-up harder.
The review states that storage stability and bioactivity must be established for manufacturing and packaging, and that very cold storage such as -80 degrees C raises equipment and access burdens.
The review argues that simpler formulations and controlled release over several days may reduce manufacturing complexity, daily gel use, and patient burden.

Only a select group of topical gels had reached human trials in the review; the authors cite limited cellular-therapy survival, unknown long-term nanoparticle effects, and the cost and duration of FDA clinical trials as barriers.

The authors conclude that topical gel treatments for diabetic foot ulcers have been studied extensively in research settings but few have been tested clinically, and they identify Regranex as the only topical gel then FDA approved specifically for DFU treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Topical gel treatments for DFUs have been studied in research settings extensively but few have been tested in the clinical setting, with only 1 topical gel (Regranex®) currently FDA approved specifically for DFU treatments.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors argue that rising DFU burden and the limited number of topical treatments should motivate development of new DFU gels.
